blocks.text: A goalkeeper takes a long goal kick and the ball traces a smooth arc across the pitch. That curve is not one complicated motion — it is two simple motions happening at the same time: a steady horizontal drift and a free fall. Separate them and every projectile question becomes two easy problems.

blocks.markdown:
A **projectile** is any body given an initial velocity and then left to move under gravity alone. Neglecting air resistance:

- **Horizontally** there is no force, so the horizontal velocity component stays **constant** and $x = u_x t$.
- **Vertically** gravity acts, so the vertical component changes at $g$ and the usual equations of motion apply.

The two motions share only one thing: the **time**. Time is the bridge you use to move between them.

blocks.title: Independence of horizontal and vertical motion
blocks.text: A bullet fired horizontally and a bullet simply dropped from the same height at the same instant hit the ground at the same time. Their vertical motions are identical because both start with zero vertical velocity and both fall under g. The forward speed changes only where they land, not when.

blocks.markdown:
### Case 1: projection horizontally from a height

Here the initial vertical velocity is zero, so the body falls exactly as if dropped.

$$h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$$

The **range** (horizontal distance) is then $R = u t$, where $u$ is the launch speed. Notice that the *time* depends only on the height, never on how fast the object was thrown forward.

blocks.title: A ball thrown horizontally off a cliff
blocks.prompt: A ball is thrown horizontally with a speed of 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², find (a) the time of flight and (b) the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff where it lands.

steps.text: Treat the vertical motion first. The ball is thrown horizontally, so its initial vertical velocity is zero.
Apply the free-fall equation for height.
Now the horizontal motion. The horizontal velocity is unchanged throughout the flight.
Substitute the launch speed and the time just found.
State the range with its unit.

blocks.answer: (a) t = 2 s  (b) R = 30 m from the foot of the cliff

blocks.markdown:
### Case 2: projection at an angle

If the body is launched with speed $u$ at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, resolve the launch velocity first:

$$u_x = u\cos\theta, \qquad u_y = u\sin\theta$$

At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero (the horizontal component is not). That single fact gives all the standard formulas.

rows: Vertical velocity falls from u sin θ to 0 at rate g
Rise and fall take equal times on level ground
From v² = u² − 2gH with v = 0 vertically
R = u cos θ × T, then use 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ
blocks.caption: Standard results for projection at an angle over level ground

blocks.title: A projectile launched at 30° to the horizontal
blocks.prompt: A stone is projected from level ground with a speed of 40 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², find (a) the maximum height reached and (b) the total time of flight.

steps.text: Resolve the launch velocity into components. Remember sin 30° = 0.5.
For (a), at the maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so use v² = u² − 2gH.
Rearrange and evaluate the maximum height.
For (b), the time to reach the top is the vertical component divided by g.
On level ground the flight is symmetrical, so double it.

blocks.title: Two angles, one range
blocks.text: Because sin 2θ = sin(180° − 2θ), complementary angles give the same range. A ball fired at 30° and one fired at 60° with the same speed land in the same place — but the 60° shot goes much higher and stays in the air much longer.

items: Resolve the launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components before anything else.
Use the vertical motion to find the time; gravity only acts vertically.
Use that time in the horizontal equation x = u cos θ × t to find the range.
At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is not.
Always state g = 10 m/s² when you use it, and attach units to every answer.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: If a projectile is launched from a height AND at an angle, you cannot use T = 2u sin θ ÷ g, because the flight is no longer symmetrical. Go back to s = ut + ½at² with downward displacement taken as the height, and solve the quadratic for t.

points: Horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent and share only the time of flight.
Horizontal velocity is constant because no horizontal force acts; vertical velocity changes at g.
For horizontal projection from a height h, t = √(2h ÷ g) and R = ut; the time does not depend on u.
For projection at angle θ: T = 2u sin θ ÷ g, H = u² sin²θ ÷ 2g and R = u² sin 2θ ÷ g.
Maximum range occurs at 45°, and complementary angles such as 30° and 60° give equal ranges.
